title: Why the French Revolution began in 1789

notes.heading: Thesis on Causes of the French Revolution
notes.body: No single cause. A financial crisis left the old system unable to function, and new ideas plus a food shortage turned a political crisis into a revolution.

source.quote: Working thesis: no single cause. A financial crisis left the old system unable to function, and new ideas plus a food shortage turned a political crisis into a revolution

notes.heading: Financial Problems
notes.body: France had huge debts, partly from wars, including its help for the American Revolution (1778-83). The tax system was unfair and messy: the First Estate (clergy) and the Second Estate (nobles) were exempt from many taxes, so the Third Estate (everyone else, about 98% of the people) paid most of them.

source.quote: France had huge debts, partly from wars, including its help for the American Revolution (1778-83). - The tax system was unfair and messy: the First Estate (clergy) and the Second Estate (nobles) were exempt from many taxes, so the Third Estate (everyone else, about 98% of the people) paid most of them

notes.heading: Resistance to Financial Reforms
notes.body: Finance ministers (Turgot, Necker, Calonne) tried reforms, and privileged groups blocked them. In 1787 the Assembly of Notables refused Calonne's tax plan.

source.quote: Finance ministers (Turgot, Necker, Calonne) tried reforms, and privileged groups blocked them. - In 1787 the Assembly of Notables refused Calonne's tax plan

notes.heading: Influence of Enlightenment Ideas
notes.body: Enlightenment writers questioned absolute monarchy and inherited privilege: Montesquieu (separation of powers), Voltaire (religious tolerance, free speech), Rousseau (popular sovereignty). Popular pamphlets spread the arguments, for example Sieyes, 'What Is the Third Estate?' (1789).

source.quote: Enlightenment writers questioned absolute monarchy and inherited privilege: Montesquieu (separation of powers), Voltaire (religious tolerance, free speech), Rousseau (popular sovereignty). - Popular pamphlets spread the arguments, for example Sieyes, "What Is the Third Estate?" (1789)

notes.heading: Impact of Hunger
notes.body: Poor harvests in 1788 pushed bread prices up sharply in 1789. Many workers spent most of their income on bread.

source.quote: Poor harvests in 1788 pushed bread prices up sharply in 1789. Many workers spent most of their income on bread

notes.heading: Key Events of 1789
notes.body: May 5: Louis XVI opened the Estates-General (the first meeting since 1614). June 17: the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. June 20: Tennis Court Oath - the deputies promised not to separate until France had a constitution. July 14: Parisians stormed the Bastille (a fortress and prison, a symbol of royal power). August 4: the Assembly abolished feudal privileges. August 26: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

source.quote: May 5: Louis XVI opened the Estates-General (the first meeting since 1614). - June 17: the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. - June 20: Tennis Court Oath - the deputies promised not to separate until France had a constitution. - July 14: Parisians stormed the Bastille (a fortress and prison, a symbol of royal power). - August 4: the Assembly abolished feudal privileges. - August 26: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
